title: They reconcile by narrowing ‘uncertain’ to lack of divine-faith certainty, and ‘doubt’ to fear
source_text: LIII. Qua in re aut sibi aperte contradicunt, aut vehementer vocibus abutuntur. Dicunt quidem ut ista inter se concilient, ut jam quoque fuit a nobis observatum, quum aiunt homines justos incertos esse, nescire, ignorare an sint in gratia, mentem suam esse quod ea de re non habeant certitudinem fidei divinae, neque istud sciant & cognoscant, quomodo res fidei noscuntur: Caeterum, dum ita loquuntur, se nolle a fidelibus & piis excludere notitiam & certitudinem moralem, aut conjecturalem, de sua apud Deum gratia atque justitia. Et similiter quum tribuunt fidelibus aliquam dubitationem de propria gratia, se non intelligere dubitationem proprie sic dictam, per quam aliquis neutri parti contradictionis audet assentiri, sed dubitationem quandam latius sumptam, quae alias in Scholis formido dici solet.
pass_a_gloss: In which matter they either openly contradict themselves, or vehemently abuse words. They say indeed, that they may reconcile these things among themselves, as has already also been observed by us, when they say that just people are uncertain, do not know, are ignorant whether they are in grace, that their meaning is that concerning that matter they do not have certainty of divine faith, nor know and cognize it as things of faith are known: But for the rest, while they so speak, they do not want to exclude from the faithful and pious moral or conjectural knowledge and certainty concerning their grace and righteousness with God. And likewise when they attribute to the faithful some doubt concerning their own grace, they do not understand doubt properly so called, by which someone dares to assent to neither part of a contradiction, but a certain doubt taken more widely, which elsewhere in the Schools is accustomed to be called fear.
pass_b_english: Their harmonizing move: ‘ignorant’ means lacking divine-faith certainty; ‘doubt’ means fear.
Le Blanc calls that either contradiction or verbal abuse.
